category.name: Containers & Kubernetes
category.description: Incidents in container platforms and Kubernetes clusters: runtime escapes, RBAC and token abuse, exposed APIs, supply chain tampering, and destructive changes.

playbooks.name: Privileged pod created outside the approved deployment path
playbooks.summary: Use when the API server audit log or a policy engine shows a pod with privileged: true, hostPID, hostNetwork, or added capabilities created by an unexpected identity.

preparation: Enforce Pod Security Admission restricted or baseline profiles on workload namespaces
Ship kube-apiserver audit logs at RequestResponse level for pod create to the SIEM
Keep an allowlist of system namespaces and service accounts permitted privileged pods
Deploy Kyverno or Gatekeeper policies that deny privileged and hostPath specs by default
identification: Pull the pod create audit event and record user, groups, source IP, and user agent
Inspect the pod spec for privileged, hostPID, hostNetwork, hostIPC, and SYS_ADMIN
Check which node the pod scheduled to and what image and command it ran
Determine whether the creating identity normally deploys via CI or GitOps
Review container logs and exec events for the pod since creation
containment: Cordon the node where the privileged pod ran to stop new scheduling
Delete the privileged pod after capturing its spec and logs as evidence
Suspend the creating identity's RoleBindings or kubeconfig credential
Apply a namespace label enforcing the restricted Pod Security profile
eradication: Inspect the node for host-level changes such as new systemd units or SSH keys
Drain and rebuild the node from a clean image if host access is suspected
Rotate service account tokens and secrets mounted on that node
recovery: Uncordon or replace the node and rebalance workloads
Confirm the admission policy now rejects the same pod spec in a dry run
Restore the identity's access with least-privilege RBAC if it was legitimate
lessons: Add a detection for privileged pod creation by non-allowlisted identities
Review why the admission policy allowed the spec, such as an exempt namespace
Track the number of namespaces running without Pod Security enforcement

splunk.title: Privileged or host-namespace pod creations
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit verb=create objectRef.resource=pods | spath path=requestObject.spec output=spec | search spec="*\"privileged\":true*" OR spec="*hostPID\":true*" OR spec="*hostNetwork\":true*" | table _time user.username sourceIPs{} objectRef.namespace objectRef.name userAgent

splunk.title: Other actions by the creating identity
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit user.username=<suspect_user> | stats count values(objectRef.namespace) as ns by verb objectRef.resource | sort - count

splunk.title: Admission denials for privileged specs after enforcement
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit objectRef.resource=pods responseStatus.code=403 "PodSecurity" | stats count by user.username objectRef.namespace

playbooks.name: Container escape to the underlying node
playbooks.summary: Use when runtime telemetry shows a container process touching host namespaces, writing to host paths, or exploiting a runtime or kernel flaw to reach the node.

preparation: Run a runtime sensor such as Falco or an EDR with container context on every node
Track container runtime, runc, and kernel versions against escape CVEs
Use seccomp RuntimeDefault and drop all capabilities in workload pod specs
Keep a golden node image so compromised nodes can be replaced quickly
identification: Review runtime alerts for nsenter, mount of host filesystems, or writes to /proc/sys
Identify the source container, pod, image digest, and node of the escape
Check the node for processes outside any container cgroup started after the alert
Determine whether the escape used a privileged spec, mounted socket, or kernel exploit
Check kubelet credentials on the node for subsequent API server use
containment: Cordon the node and isolate it with a cloud security group or network policy
Snapshot the node disk and capture memory before termination
Revoke the node's kubelet client certificate or cloud instance role sessions
Block the source image digest via admission policy
eradication: Terminate the node and replace it from the golden image
Patch runc, containerd, and the kernel across the node pool
Rotate secrets that were mounted into any pod scheduled on the node
recovery: Redeploy workloads onto patched nodes and verify health
Confirm runtime sensors are reporting from all replacement nodes
Review the image source and rebuild it from a trusted base
lessons: Measure patch lag on node images for container runtime CVEs
Add detections for host namespace entry from container processes
Evaluate sandboxed runtimes such as gVisor or Kata for untrusted workloads

splunk.title: Falco escape-related rules by node and pod
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=falco (rule="*Namespace*" OR rule="*Mount*" OR rule="*Escape*" OR rule="*Sensitive*mount*") | stats count values(output_fields.proc.cmdline) as cmds by output_fields.k8s.pod.name output_fields.k8s.ns.name hostname rule

splunk.title: API calls using the node's kubelet identity
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit user.username="system:node:<node_name>" NOT verb IN (get,watch,list) | stats count by verb objectRef.resource objectRef.namespace

splunk.title: Host processes outside containers on the node
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.dest=<node_name> by Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.user _time span=1m | sort - _time

playbooks.name: Kubelet API exposed and accessed anonymously
playbooks.summary: Use when a node's kubelet port 10250 or read-only 10255 is reachable from untrusted networks with anonymous auth, allowing pod listing or command execution.

preparation: Set kubelet anonymous-auth false and authorization-mode Webhook on every node
Disable the kubelet read-only port 10255 in the node configuration
Restrict node security groups so 10250 is only reachable from the control plane
Log kubelet authentication failures and node flow logs to the SIEM
identification: Scan node IPs from an external host to confirm whether 10250 or 10255 respond
Review VPC or firewall flow logs for external sources connecting to kubelet ports
Check kubelet logs for /run, /exec, or /pods requests from unknown sources
List containers that had commands run via the kubelet and the commands executed
Confirm the kubelet configuration flags on affected nodes
containment: Block inbound 10250 and 10255 from the internet at the security group or firewall
Cordon affected nodes and restart kubelet with anonymous auth disabled
Terminate pods that had commands executed through the kubelet
eradication: Replace affected nodes and fix the node bootstrap template or launch configuration
Rotate secrets and tokens from pods where commands ran
Remove miners or tools dropped into containers via kubelet exec
recovery: Verify from outside that kubelet ports are unreachable on all nodes
Confirm kubectl logs and exec still work through the API server
Re-run CIS Kubernetes Benchmark checks on the node pool
lessons: Add continuous external exposure scanning for kubelet ports
Review how the node template drifted from hardened defaults
Alert on any direct kubelet API call not originating from the API server

splunk.title: Inbound connections to kubelet ports from outside the cluster
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (10250,10255) All_Traffic.action=allowed NOT All_Traffic.src IN (<control_plane_cidrs>) by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port

splunk.title: VPC flow log hits on kubelet ports
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=aws:cloudwatchlogs:vpcflow dest_port IN (10250,10255) action=ACCEPT | stats count earliest(_time) as first latest(_time) as last by src_ip dest_ip | convert ctime(first) ctime(last)

splunk.title: Kubelet exec and run requests
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:kubelet ("/exec/" OR "/run/" OR "/pods") | rex "(?<path>/(exec|run|pods)[^ \"]*)" | stats count by host path

playbooks.name: Docker daemon socket or remote API exposed
playbooks.summary: Use when the Docker API on TCP 2375/2376 is reachable without TLS auth, or docker.sock is mounted into a container, letting someone start containers on the host.

preparation: Disable the Docker TCP listener or require mutual TLS on port 2376
Block mounts of /var/run/docker.sock in workloads via admission policy
Forward docker events and daemon logs to the SIEM
Inventory hosts running dockerd outside the managed cluster
identification: Confirm external reachability of 2375 and 2376 on the host
Pull docker events for container create, start, and exec in the exposure window
List running containers with their images, mounts, and creation times
Identify containers mounting / or docker.sock from the host
Check outbound connections from new containers for mining pools or C2
containment: Firewall off the Docker API port and stop the TCP listener
Stop and preserve unknown containers with docker export before removal
Isolate the host from the network if a host mount was used
eradication: Remove unknown containers, images, and volumes created by the attacker
Check host crontabs, authorized_keys, and systemd units for persistence
Rebuild the host if the root filesystem was mounted into an attacker container
recovery: Restore legitimate containers from known image digests
Verify the daemon configuration file no longer exposes tcp://0.0.0.0
Confirm from an external host that 2375 and 2376 no longer answer
lessons: Add external scanning for 2375 and 2376 across all public ranges
Detect docker.sock mounts in pod specs and compose files
Review why the host was outside configuration management

splunk.title: Container creates and execs from docker events
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=docker:events (Action=create OR Action=start OR Action=exec_create*) host=<host> | table _time Action Actor.Attributes.image Actor.Attributes.name Actor.ID

splunk.title: Connections to Docker API ports
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (2375,2376) by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.action | sort - count

splunk.title: Images pulled during exposure window
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=docker:events Type=image Action=pull host=<host> | stats earliest(_time) as first by Actor.ID Actor.Attributes.name | convert ctime(first)

playbooks.name: Cryptominer running in the cluster
playbooks.summary: Use when nodes show sustained CPU saturation, connections to mining pools, or runtime alerts for miner binaries inside pods or as host processes.

preparation: Set CPU limits and ResourceQuotas on every namespace
Restrict egress with NetworkPolicies or an egress gateway so pods cannot reach arbitrary ports
Subscribe to a threat feed of mining pool domains and stratum ports for DNS and proxy logs
Alert on cloud bill anomalies for node autoscaling
identification: Find pods and nodes with sustained near-limit CPU usage and unexpected images
Check DNS logs for mining pool domains and connections on stratum ports such as 3333 or 4444
Identify the workload controller that created the miner pod, such as a Deployment or CronJob
Trace how the miner arrived: exposed dashboard, vulnerable app, stolen kubeconfig, or image
Check for DaemonSets that spread the miner to every node
containment: Scale the malicious workload to zero and preserve its manifest
Apply a deny-all egress NetworkPolicy to the affected namespace
Block mining pool domains at DNS and egress firewall
Revoke the credential used to deploy the miner
eradication: Delete the miner workloads, CronJobs, and any DaemonSets they created
Patch the vulnerable application or exposed component that was the entry point
Check nodes for host-level miner persistence outside Kubernetes
recovery: Scale down autoscaled nodes added during mining
Confirm cluster CPU usage returns to baseline
Re-deploy affected legitimate workloads from GitOps
lessons: Add detection for pods connecting to stratum ports or pool domains
Review cost impact and whether billing alerts fired in time
Track namespaces without egress restrictions

splunk.title: DNS lookups for mining pools from cluster CIDRs
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=stream:dns src_ip IN (<pod_cidrs>) (query="*pool*" OR query="*xmr*" OR query="*monero*" OR query="*nanopool*") | stats count by src_ip query

splunk.title: Outbound connections on stratum ports
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (3333,4444,5555,7777,14444) All_Traffic.src IN (<pod_cidrs>,<node_cidrs>) by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port

splunk.title: Who created the miner workload
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit verb=create objectRef.resource IN (deployments,daemonsets,cronjobs,pods) objectRef.namespace=<namespace> | table _time user.username sourceIPs{} objectRef.resource objectRef.name userAgent

playbooks.name: Malicious or typosquatted image pulled from a public registry
playbooks.summary: Use when a workload runs an image from Docker Hub or another public registry that is unvetted, typosquatted, or contains miners, backdoors, or credential stealers.

preparation: Allow images only from the internal registry or a pull-through cache via admission policy
Scan images in the registry and at admission for malware and known CVEs
Require image references by digest in production manifests
Keep an SBOM and provenance attestation for each internal base image
identification: List all pods running the suspect image name or digest across clusters
Compare the image name with the intended one for typosquatting such as alpline or nginxx
Pull the image into an isolated sandbox and inspect layers, entrypoint, and embedded binaries
Check which manifest, Helm chart, or developer introduced the image reference
Review network connections and processes from containers using the image
containment: Add the image digest and repository to an admission deny policy
Scale down or delete workloads using the image after preserving manifests
Block egress destinations contacted by the image's processes
eradication: Replace the image reference with a vetted internal image pinned by digest
Rotate secrets and service account tokens available to the affected pods
Purge the image from node caches and the pull-through cache
recovery: Redeploy affected services and verify functionality
Confirm admission now rejects pulls from unapproved public registries
Notify the public registry of the malicious repository
lessons: Track the percentage of running images from approved registries
Add a CI check for image names close to popular images
Review whether developers had a fast path to request new base images

splunk.title: Pods created with the suspect image
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit verb=create objectRef.resource=pods "<suspect_image>" | table _time user.username objectRef.namespace objectRef.name

splunk.title: Container runtime image pulls from public registries
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:container:* OR sourcetype=docker:events Action=pull | rex field=_raw "(?<image>(docker\.io|ghcr\.io|quay\.io)/[^\s\"]+)" | stats count by image host | sort - count

splunk.title: Network activity from pods running the image
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=falco output_fields.container.image.repository=<suspect_repo> | stats count values(output_fields.fd.name) as conns by rule output_fields.k8s.pod.name

playbooks.name: Kubernetes secrets read in bulk or etcd accessed directly
playbooks.summary: Use when audit logs show an identity listing or getting many secrets across namespaces, or someone connects directly to etcd and dumps the keyspace.

preparation: Enable envelope encryption for secrets at rest with a KMS provider
Restrict etcd client ports 2379 and 2380 to control plane nodes with mTLS
Audit secrets get, list, and watch at Metadata level or higher
Limit RBAC so few identities can list secrets cluster-wide
identification: Find identities that performed list or get on secrets across many namespaces
Record which secret names were read and classify them by system and sensitivity
Check etcd logs and network flows for client connections from non control-plane IPs
Determine whether the identity is a human, CI system, operator, or stolen token
Check whether etcd backups or snapshots were copied off-cluster
containment: Remove the identity's RBAC permission on secrets or disable the credential
Firewall etcd ports to control plane addresses only
Prioritise rotation of cloud keys, database passwords, and TLS keys found in read secrets
eradication: Rotate every secret read by the identity and update dependent workloads
Rotate etcd client certificates and the KMS encryption key if etcd was dumped
Hunt for use of the stolen secrets in cloud, database, and SaaS logs
recovery: Restart workloads to pick up rotated secrets and confirm health
Verify encryption at rest is active by reading a secret directly from etcd as a test
Secure etcd backup storage with access logging and encryption
lessons: Add a detection for secrets list across more than a few namespaces by one identity
Move high-value secrets to an external secret manager with per-read audit
Measure time to rotate all secrets in a namespace

splunk.title: Identities reading secrets across many namespaces
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit objectRef.resource=secrets verb IN (get,list,watch) | stats dc(objectRef.namespace) as namespaces dc(objectRef.name) as secrets count by user.username sourceIPs{} | where namespaces>3 | sort - secrets

splunk.title: Secrets read by the suspect identity
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit objectRef.resource=secrets user.username=<suspect_user> | stats count by objectRef.namespace objectRef.name verb

splunk.title: Connections to etcd from outside the control plane
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (2379,2380) NOT All_Traffic.src IN (<control_plane_ips>) by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest

playbooks.name: Service account token stolen and used outside its pod
playbooks.summary: Use when a Kubernetes service account token is used from an unexpected IP, user agent, or for actions the workload never performs, suggesting it was exfiltrated.

preparation: Use projected, time-bound service account tokens instead of legacy secret tokens
Set automountServiceAccountToken false for workloads that do not call the API
Restrict API server access to known CIDRs or a private endpoint
Baseline each service account's normal verbs, resources, and source IPs
identification: Find audit events for the service account from source IPs outside the pod CIDR
Compare user agents with the workload's normal client library
List actions the token performed that the workload never needs, such as listing secrets
Identify the pod or legacy secret the token came from and how it leaked
Check whether the token was used to create new tokens or RoleBindings
containment: Delete the legacy token secret or restart the pod to invalidate its projected token
Temporarily remove the service account's RoleBindings
Block the external source IP from the API server endpoint
eradication: Recreate the service account and rebind only the permissions it needs
Remove any tokens, RoleBindings, or workloads the attacker created
Fix the leak path, such as a token in logs, image layers, or an SSRF in the app
recovery: Redeploy the workload with the new service account and verify API calls succeed
Confirm no further API calls from the external IP
Verify the workload now mounts only a projected, audience-bound token
lessons: Add an alert for service accounts used from outside pod and node CIDRs
Migrate remaining legacy service account token secrets
Review RBAC to remove wildcard verbs from workload service accounts

splunk.title: Service account calls from outside cluster networks
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit user.username="system:serviceaccount:*" | mvexpand sourceIPs{} | rename sourceIPs{} as src | search NOT src IN (<pod_cidrs>,<node_cidrs>) | stats count values(verb) as verbs by user.username src userAgent

splunk.title: Actions by the suspect service account
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit user.username="system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<sa_name>" | stats count by verb objectRef.resource objectRef.namespace responseStatus.code | sort - count

splunk.title: Token or RoleBinding creation by the service account
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit user.username="system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<sa_name>" (objectRef.subresource=token OR objectRef.resource IN (rolebindings,clusterrolebindings,serviceaccounts)) verb=create

playbooks.name: Unexpected cluster-admin ClusterRoleBinding created
playbooks.summary: Use when a ClusterRoleBinding or RoleBinding granting cluster-admin or wildcard permissions appears for a user, group, or service account outside change control.

preparation: Manage all RBAC bindings through GitOps so drift is detectable
Alert on any create or patch of ClusterRoleBindings referencing cluster-admin
Limit bind and escalate verbs to a break-glass group
identification: Pull the binding create event with the subject, roleRef, and creating identity
Check whether the binding exists in the GitOps repo or a change ticket
Review all actions taken by the newly bound subject since the binding
Determine how the creating identity had permission to bind cluster-admin
Search for other bindings, ClusterRoles, or webhooks created in the same session
containment: Delete the unauthorised binding after exporting its YAML
Disable the creating identity's credential or revoke its kubeconfig certificate
Disable the newly privileged subject if it is attacker controlled
eradication: Remove any workloads, webhooks, or CRDs created with the elevated access
Rotate cluster secrets read by the privileged subject
Reconcile RBAC against the GitOps source of truth and remove drift
recovery: Confirm the GitOps controller reports RBAC in sync
Verify break-glass access still works for the platform team
Re-run an RBAC review tool to list remaining cluster-admin subjects
lessons: Count identities able to bind or escalate and reduce them
Add policy blocking cluster-admin bindings outside the platform namespace pipeline
Review time from binding creation to detection

splunk.title: ClusterRoleBinding creates and patches
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit objectRef.resource IN (clusterrolebindings,rolebindings) verb IN (create,update,patch) | spath path=requestObject.roleRef.name output=role | spath path=requestObject.subjects{}.name output=subject | table _time user.username verb objectRef.name role subject sourceIPs{}

splunk.title: Actions by the newly bound subject
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit user.username=<bound_subject> earliest=<binding_time> | stats count by verb objectRef.resource objectRef.namespace | sort - count

splunk.title: Admission webhooks or CRDs created in the same window
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit verb=create objectRef.resource IN (mutatingwebhookconfigurations,validatingwebhookconfigurations,customresourcedefinitions,clusterroles) earliest=<binding_time> | table _time user.username objectRef.resource objectRef.name

playbooks.name: Admission controller or policy engine disabled or bypassed
playbooks.summary: Use when Gatekeeper, Kyverno, or a validating webhook is deleted, set to fail open, or has namespaces excluded, removing guardrails on what can run in the cluster.

preparation: Set policy webhooks to failurePolicy Fail for security-critical rules
Alert on deletes or changes to ValidatingWebhookConfiguration and policy CRDs
Protect the policy engine namespace with RBAC limited to the platform team
identification: Find the delete or patch on webhook configurations, Kyverno policies, or Gatekeeper constraints
Check whether failurePolicy changed to Ignore or namespaceSelector excluded namespaces
Check whether the policy engine pods were scaled to zero or crash-looping
List resources created during the gap that the policy would have rejected
Identify the identity that made the change and whether a ticket covers it
containment: Restore the webhook and policy objects from the GitOps repository
Scale the policy engine back up and confirm it is admitting requests
Suspend the identity that disabled the controls pending review
eradication: Delete or remediate non-compliant workloads admitted during the gap
Rerun the policy engine audit mode to report existing violations
Remove namespace exclusions or Ignore failure policies added to the webhook
recovery: Confirm a known-bad test manifest is rejected in each protected namespace
Confirm the GitOps controller self-heals policy objects on drift
Check policy engine resource limits to prevent future crash-loop gaps
lessons: Alert when policy webhook endpoints are unavailable for more than a few minutes
Review who can modify webhook configurations and why
Track admitted-during-gap resources as a metric

splunk.title: Changes to webhook configurations and policy objects
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit objectRef.resource IN (validatingwebhookconfigurations,mutatingwebhookconfigurations,clusterpolicies,policies,constrainttemplates) verb IN (delete,patch,update) | table _time user.username verb objectRef.resource objectRef.name sourceIPs{}

splunk.title: Policy engine deployment scaled or deleted
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit objectRef.namespace IN (kyverno,gatekeeper-system) objectRef.resource IN (deployments,pods) verb IN (delete,patch,update) | table _time user.username verb objectRef.name objectRef.subresource

splunk.title: Privileged workloads created during the gap
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit verb=create objectRef.resource=pods earliest=<gap_start> latest=<gap_end> ("privileged\":true" OR "hostPath") | table _time user.username objectRef.namespace objectRef.name

playbooks.name: Gap in Kubernetes API server audit logs
playbooks.summary: Use when kube-apiserver audit events stop arriving, drop sharply, or the audit policy is weakened, leaving a window where cluster activity cannot be reconstructed.

preparation: Alert when audit event volume per cluster drops below a baseline for 15 minutes
Keep the audit policy file under version control with change review
For managed clusters, enable control plane audit log export to the cloud logging service
Monitor the log forwarder DaemonSet or webhook backend health
identification: Chart audit event count per cluster to find the exact gap start and end
Check whether the audit policy file or API server flags changed before the gap
Check log forwarder pods, buffers, and SIEM ingestion errors for the same window
For EKS, AKS, or GKE, check whether control plane logging was disabled via the cloud API
Use other sources such as node logs, cloud trail, and GitOps history to cover the gap
containment: Restore the audit policy and logging configuration from version control
Re-enable managed control plane log export and confirm events arrive
Restrict who can modify cluster logging settings in the cloud account
eradication: Diff cluster state, RBAC, and workloads against GitOps to spot changes made in the gap
Remove resources created in the gap that have no change record
Revert unauthorised audit policy edits on control plane nodes and restart the API server
recovery: Backfill buffered audit logs from the forwarder or cloud log store if retained
Verify event volume and field parsing are back to normal
Document the unrecoverable window in the incident record
lessons: Add a heartbeat search for each cluster's audit stream
Add a detection for cloud API calls that disable cluster logging
Review buffer sizes so forwarder restarts do not lose events

splunk.title: Audit event volume per cluster
splunk.spl: | tstats count where index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit by _time span=5m host | timechart span=5m sum(count) by host

splunk.title: Managed cluster logging disabled via cloud API
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventSource=eks.amazonaws.com eventName=UpdateClusterConfig | spath path=requestParameters.logging output=logging | table _time userIdentity.arn requestParameters.name logging sourceIPAddress

splunk.title: Clusters with no audit events in the last 30 minutes
splunk.spl: | tstats latest(_time) as last where index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit by host | eval mins_since=round((now()-last)/60) | where mins_since>30

playbooks.name: Interactive exec into a production pod
playbooks.summary: Use when someone runs kubectl exec or attach into a production pod outside break-glass procedure, possibly to read secrets, alter data, or install tools.

preparation: Restrict pods/exec and pods/attach RBAC in production to a break-glass group
Log exec sessions with command capture through a session recording proxy or runtime sensor
Define a break-glass request process with ticket and approver
identification: Find pods/exec create events in production namespaces with user and source IP
Match the exec to a break-glass ticket or on-call incident
Pull runtime sensor events for commands run in the shell session
Check whether the session read mounted secrets or environment variables
Check whether files were written or packages installed in the container filesystem
containment: Restart the pod to discard any changes made in the container filesystem
Remove the user's exec permission until the review completes
Revoke the user's kubeconfig credential if the session is unexplained
eradication: Rotate secrets the session could read from mounts or environment
Revert data or configuration changes made through the shell
Remove tools or binaries the session left on persistent volumes
recovery: Confirm the restarted pod is healthy and running the expected image
Restore exec permission through the break-glass group only
Reconcile application data touched in the session against backups or replicas
lessons: Alert on any exec in production without a linked ticket
Review what task required a shell and provide a safer tool for it
Report exec counts per team monthly

splunk.title: Exec and attach into production namespaces
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit objectRef.subresource IN (exec,attach) objectRef.namespace IN (<prod_namespaces>) verb=create | table _time user.username sourceIPs{} objectRef.namespace objectRef.name requestURI

splunk.title: Commands spawned in the exec'd container
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=falco output_fields.k8s.pod.name=<pod_name> (rule="Terminal shell in container" OR rule="*Read sensitive file*" OR rule="*Package management*") | table _time rule output_fields.proc.cmdline output_fields.user.name

splunk.title: Exec users without matching break-glass tickets
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit objectRef.subresource=exec objectRef.namespace IN (<prod_namespaces>) | stats count by user.username | lookup breakglass_approvals user AS user.username OUTPUT ticket | where isnull(ticket)

playbooks.name: Malicious sidecar injected through a mutating webhook
playbooks.summary: Use when pods gain unexpected containers, init containers, or env vars at admission because a mutating webhook was added or tampered with to inject a backdoor sidecar.

preparation: Inventory approved mutating webhooks such as service mesh injectors with their CA bundles
Alert on create or patch of MutatingWebhookConfiguration objects
Compare running pod container lists against rendered manifests in CI
identification: List MutatingWebhookConfigurations and flag any not in the approved inventory
Diff a running pod's containers against its Deployment manifest in Git
Identify the webhook service endpoint and the pod serving it
Inspect the injected sidecar image, command, and network destinations
Determine how many namespaces and pods received the sidecar
containment: Delete the rogue MutatingWebhookConfiguration after exporting it
Scale down the webhook server deployment and preserve its image
Block egress from injected sidecars to their destinations
eradication: Rolling-restart every affected workload so pods are recreated without the sidecar
Rotate secrets and tokens visible to injected pods
Remove the RBAC that allowed creating webhook configurations
recovery: Confirm pod specs match Git-rendered manifests after restart
Verify legitimate injectors such as the service mesh still function
Confirm only approved webhooks remain in the cluster webhook inventory
lessons: Add a continuous check for pods with containers absent from their owner spec
Pin webhook configurations in GitOps with self-heal enabled
Review supply chain for the webhook server image

splunk.title: Mutating webhook configuration changes
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit objectRef.resource=mutatingwebhookconfigurations verb IN (create,update,patch) | table _time user.username verb objectRef.name sourceIPs{}

splunk.title: Pod creates mutated by an unexpected webhook
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit verb=create objectRef.resource=pods | spath path=annotations output=ann | search ann="*mutation.webhook.admission.k8s.io*" | rex field=ann "\"mutation.webhook.admission.k8s.io/round_\d+_index_\d+\":\"(?<mutation>[^\"]+)" | stats count by mutation objectRef.namespace

splunk.title: Network connections from the injected sidecar
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=falco output_fields.container.name=<sidecar_name> | stats count values(output_fields.fd.name) as conns by output_fields.k8s.ns.name output_fields.k8s.pod.name

playbooks.name: Helm chart or chart repository tampered with
playbooks.summary: Use when a Helm chart in an internal or third-party repository was modified to add malicious templates, hooks, or images, or a release was upgraded with unexpected values.

preparation: Sign charts with Helm provenance or cosign and verify at install
Mirror third-party charts into an internal OCI registry with pinned versions
Restrict who can push to the internal chart repository
identification: Diff the deployed chart version against the last known good version from the repo
Inspect templates for new hooks, Jobs, ClusterRoles, or images
Check chart repository push logs for who uploaded the tampered version
List releases in all clusters using the tampered chart version
Review helm release history secrets for unexpected upgrades and values
containment: Remove the tampered chart version from the repository and block its digest
Roll back affected releases to the last known good revision
Revoke the credential used to push the chart
eradication: Delete resources created by malicious hooks, which helm rollback may not remove
Rotate secrets exposed to the malicious templates
Rebuild and re-sign the chart from verified source
recovery: Redeploy releases from the re-signed chart and confirm signature verification
Verify release workloads match expected images and RBAC
Restore chart repository push access only to the release pipeline identity
lessons: Enforce signature verification in CI and GitOps for every chart install
Add alerting on chart repo pushes outside the release pipeline
Review how many third-party charts are pulled directly from the internet

splunk.title: Helm release secret changes
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit objectRef.resource=secrets objectRef.name="sh.helm.release.v1.*" verb IN (create,update) | table _time user.username objectRef.namespace objectRef.name userAgent

splunk.title: Resources created by helm hook Jobs
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit verb=create objectRef.namespace=<release_namespace> earliest=<upgrade_time> latest=<upgrade_time_plus_1h> | stats count by user.username objectRef.resource objectRef.name

splunk.title: Pushes to the chart repository
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=<registry_sourcetype> action=push (artifact_type=helm OR repository="charts/*") | table _time user repository tag digest src_ip

playbooks.name: Container registry credentials leaked
playbooks.summary: Use when an imagePullSecret, registry robot account token, or cloud registry key is exposed in a repo, log, or image, risking image tampering or private image theft.

preparation: Use short-lived registry auth via workload identity rather than static pull secrets
Scope robot accounts to pull-only per project
Enable registry audit logs for pull, push, and delete with source IP
Run secret scanning on repositories and container image layers
identification: Identify which registry account leaked and its permissions such as push or delete
Find where the credential was exposed and since when
Review registry audit logs for that account from unexpected IPs
Check for pushes that overwrote existing tags in the exposure window
List private repositories pulled by the account from unknown sources
containment: Revoke or rotate the leaked registry token or robot account
Enable tag immutability on production repositories
Remove the credential from the exposed repo, log, or image and purge history
eradication: Compare digests of production tags against CI build records and rebuild mismatches
Update imagePullSecrets in every namespace with the new credential
Delete any images pushed by the attacker
recovery: Restart workloads that pull with the new credential and confirm pulls succeed
Verify running pods use digests produced by CI
Confirm the old token returns unauthorised against the registry API
lessons: Add an alert on registry pushes from outside CI runners
Measure how many clusters still use static pull secrets
Review why the secret scanner did not catch the exposure

splunk.title: Registry API activity by leaked identity
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventSource=ecr.amazonaws.com userIdentity.arn=<leaked_identity_arn> | stats count by eventName sourceIPAddress requestParameters.repositoryName

splunk.title: Image pushes overwriting existing tags
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventSource=ecr.amazonaws.com eventName=PutImage | spath path=requestParameters.imageTag output=tag | stats dc(responseElements.image.imageId.imageDigest) as digests values(userIdentity.arn) as who by requestParameters.repositoryName tag | where digests>1

splunk.title: Pull secrets referencing the leaked registry account
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit objectRef.resource=secrets verb IN (create,update) "kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson" | table _time user.username objectRef.namespace objectRef.name

playbooks.name: Node compromised through a hostPath volume mount
playbooks.summary: Use when a pod mounts sensitive host paths such as /, /etc, /var/lib/kubelet, or /root and uses them to read credentials or plant persistence on the node.

preparation: Deny hostPath volumes in workload namespaces via Pod Security or policy engine
Allowlist the few system DaemonSets that need specific read-only host paths
Run file integrity monitoring on node paths such as /etc/systemd, /root/.ssh, and /etc/cron.d
identification: Find pods created with hostPath volumes and list the host paths and readOnly flags
Check runtime events for reads of /var/lib/kubelet/pki or other pods' token directories
Look for writes to host crontabs, systemd units, or authorized_keys from the container
Identify every node where pods with that spec were scheduled
Check for API calls using the node's kubelet credentials after the mount
containment: Delete the hostPath pod and cordon affected nodes
Revoke kubelet client certificates for affected nodes
Block SSH and outbound traffic from affected nodes except to forensics tooling
eradication: Replace affected nodes rather than cleaning them in place
Rotate tokens and secrets of every pod that ran on affected nodes
Remove the RBAC or namespace exemption that allowed hostPath
recovery: Reschedule workloads to fresh nodes and validate health
Confirm the policy rejects hostPath in a test namespace
Re-enable node autoscaling with the hardened node template
lessons: Add detection for hostPath mounts of root, kubelet, or runtime sockets
Review DaemonSets with broad host mounts and reduce them
Track time to replace a compromised node pool

splunk.title: Pods created with hostPath volumes
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit verb=create objectRef.resource=pods "hostPath" | spath path=requestObject.spec.volumes{}.hostPath.path output=host_paths | table _time user.username objectRef.namespace objectRef.name host_paths

splunk.title: Sensitive host file writes from containers
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=falco (output_fields.fd.name="/host/etc/*" OR output_fields.fd.name="*/.ssh/authorized_keys" OR output_fields.fd.name="*/var/lib/kubelet/*" OR rule="*Write below etc*") | table _time hostname rule output_fields.k8s.pod.name output_fields.fd.name output_fields.proc.cmdline

splunk.title: Node identity API usage after the mount
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit user.username="system:node:*" objectRef.resource=secrets | stats count dc(objectRef.namespace) as ns by user.username sourceIPs{}

playbooks.name: Argo CD or GitOps repository compromised
playbooks.summary: Use when unauthorised commits land in a GitOps config repo, or the Argo CD or Flux controller is accessed, so the cluster syncs attacker-chosen manifests.

preparation: Require signed commits and protected branches with review on GitOps repos
Put the Argo CD UI and API behind SSO with MFA, not the local admin account
Forward Argo CD audit events and Git provider audit logs to the SIEM
Scope Argo CD Projects so each app can only deploy to its own namespaces
identification: Identify commits to the GitOps repo outside the normal pipeline or by unexpected authors
Check Argo CD logs for logins, especially the admin account, and app or project changes
Diff synced manifests to find new images, RBAC, webhooks, or CronJobs
Check whether Argo CD repository credentials or cluster secrets were viewed or exported
List clusters and namespaces that synced the malicious revision
containment: Disable auto-sync on affected Argo CD applications
Revert the malicious commits and force a sync to the last known good revision
Disable the local admin account and revoke compromised Git and Argo CD tokens
Restrict the Argo CD API endpoint to the corporate network or VPN
eradication: Delete orphaned resources created by the malicious sync that pruning missed
Rotate Git deploy keys, Argo CD repo credentials, and cluster bearer tokens it stores
Review the Git provider account that pushed the commits for wider compromise
recovery: Re-enable auto-sync after verifying every app is in sync with reviewed Git
Confirm branch protection and signature checks block an unsigned test commit
Validate application health across all synced clusters
lessons: Alert on commits to GitOps repos not signed by the pipeline or approved keys
Review Argo CD Project scoping that let one app deploy cluster-wide resources
Add Argo CD admin login detection

splunk.title: Argo CD logins and application changes
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:container:argocd-server ("login" OR "update" OR "sync" OR "delete") | rex "user=(?<user>\S+)" | rex "application=(?<app>\S+)" | stats count values(app) as apps by user

splunk.title: Resources applied by the Argo CD controller during the window
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit user.username="system:serviceaccount:argocd:argocd-application-controller" verb IN (create,patch,update) earliest=<commit_time> | stats count by objectRef.resource objectRef.namespace objectRef.name

splunk.title: Pushes to the GitOps repository
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=github:audit OR sourcetype=gitlab:audit repo=<gitops_repo> (action=git.push OR action=protected_branch.*) | table _time actor action repo branch actor_ip

playbooks.name: Managed cluster (EKS, AKS, GKE) control-plane credential leaked
playbooks.summary: Use when a kubeconfig, cloud key, or IAM role with access to a managed Kubernetes control plane is exposed and may be used to gain cluster admin through the cloud identity mapping.

preparation: Use EKS access entries, AKS Entra ID RBAC, or GKE IAM rather than shared static kubeconfigs
Make the managed API endpoint private or restrict public access CIDRs
Disable AKS local accounts and avoid GKE client certificate auth
Keep cloud audit logs for cluster API calls such as DescribeCluster and ListClusterUserCredential
identification: Identify the leaked credential type and which cloud principal and cluster it maps to
Search cloud audit logs for credential retrieval calls by the principal from unknown IPs
Search kube audit logs for the mapped username and groups from the same source IPs
Check for changes to access entries, aws-auth ConfigMap, or role assignments
List workloads, secrets, and RBAC changed by the identity
containment: Disable or rotate the cloud access key, or revoke the role session
Remove the principal's cluster access entry or role assignment
Restrict the public API endpoint to known CIDRs immediately
Rotate the cluster CA or reset credentials if a client certificate or local admin leaked
eradication: Remove persistence such as new access entries, aws-auth mappings, or ClusterRoleBindings
Delete attacker workloads and rotate secrets read during the session
Check the cloud account for other actions by the leaked principal beyond the cluster
recovery: Reissue kubeconfigs via SSO-backed cloud CLI auth to legitimate users
Confirm CI pipelines authenticate using workload identity federation
Verify the public endpoint restriction does not break operators
lessons: Alert on cluster credential retrieval from new IPs or ASNs
Inventory clusters with local accounts or static kubeconfigs and remove them
Review where the credential was stored and why it was long-lived

splunk.title: EKS credential and access entry calls by the principal
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventSource=eks.amazonaws.com userIdentity.arn=<leaked_principal_arn> | stats count by eventName sourceIPAddress requestParameters.name | sort - count

splunk.title: AKS user credential retrieval
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=azure:monitor:activity operationName.value="Microsoft.ContainerService/managedClusters/listClusterUserCredential/action" OR operationName.value="Microsoft.ContainerService/managedClusters/listClusterAdminCredential/action" | table _time caller callerIpAddress resourceId

splunk.title: Cluster actions by mapped identity from new IPs
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit user.username=<mapped_username> | mvexpand sourceIPs{} | stats count values(verb) as verbs earliest(_time) as first by sourceIPs{} | convert ctime(first)

splunk.title: aws-auth ConfigMap or access entry changes
splunk.spl: index=* (sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit objectRef.name=aws-auth objectRef.namespace=kube-system verb IN (update,patch)) OR (sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventName IN (CreateAccessEntry,AssociateAccessPolicy)) | table _time sourcetype user.username userIdentity.arn eventName

playbooks.name: Falco runtime alert: shell or suspicious process in container
playbooks.summary: Use to triage a Falco or similar runtime detection such as a shell spawned in a container, unexpected outbound connection, or sensitive file read, and decide if it is malicious.

preparation: Tune Falco rules with workload-specific allowlists to keep alert volume reviewable
Ship Falco events with Kubernetes metadata fields to the SIEM
Map each namespace to an owning team and on-call contact
identification: Read the Falco rule, output fields, process tree, and container image
Check whether the parent process is the app, an exec session, or a CronJob
Correlate with kube audit for exec events into the same pod at the same time
Look for follow-on alerts on the pod such as outbound connections or package installs
Ask the owning team whether the behaviour matches a known job or debug action
containment: Apply a deny-egress NetworkPolicy label to the pod if behaviour is unexplained
Capture container filesystem diff and process list before deletion
Delete the pod and let its controller recreate it from the clean image
eradication: Patch the application vulnerability if the shell came from the app process
Rebuild the image if malicious content is present in its layers
Rotate credentials mounted into the pod
recovery: Confirm the recreated pod shows no repeat alert
Remove the temporary deny-egress label once clean
Add a tuned exception if the alert was confirmed benign
lessons: Track true and false positive rates per Falco rule
Record time from runtime alert to owner acknowledgement
Consider read-only root filesystems to make shells less useful

splunk.title: Falco alerts by rule, namespace, and image
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=falco priority IN (Critical,Error,Warning) | stats count values(output_fields.proc.cmdline) as cmds by rule output_fields.k8s.ns.name output_fields.container.image.repository | sort - count

splunk.title: All runtime events for the alerting pod
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=falco output_fields.k8s.pod.name=<pod_name> | table _time rule output_fields.proc.pname output_fields.proc.cmdline output_fields.fd.name

splunk.title: Exec events matching the alert time
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit objectRef.subresource=exec objectRef.name=<pod_name> | table _time user.username sourceIPs{} requestURI

playbooks.name: Namespace deleted or mass resource deletion in the cluster
playbooks.summary: Use when namespaces, deployments, PVCs, or CRDs are deleted in bulk, by mistake or maliciously, causing outages or data loss in the cluster.

preparation: Back up cluster resources and persistent volumes with Velero or a managed equivalent
Set PersistentVolume reclaim policy to Retain for stateful data
Restrict delete on namespaces and CRDs to a small platform group
Use GitOps so stateless workloads can be re-synced quickly
identification: Find delete and deletecollection events and the identity, source IP, and user agent
List deleted namespaces, PVCs, and CRDs and their owning services
Determine whether the actor is a person, CI job, operator, or stolen credential
Check whether retained PersistentVolumes or cloud disks still exist
Check for preceding malicious activity such as new bindings or secrets reads
containment: Revoke the deleting identity's credential or RBAC immediately
Pause GitOps pruning and CI pipelines that might delete more
Snapshot cloud disks backing released PersistentVolumes
eradication: Remove any attacker-created RBAC or workloads found during review
Fix the automation or script that issued the deletes if it was an error
Add finalizer or policy protection for critical namespaces
recovery: Restore namespaces and resources from the latest Velero backup
Rebind restored PVCs to retained volumes or restore data from snapshots
Re-sync stateless apps from GitOps and verify service health
Communicate data loss window to service owners
lessons: Measure restore time against the recovery time objective
Add an alert for deletes of more than a few resources by one identity in minutes
Run regular restore tests for cluster backups

splunk.title: Bulk deletes by identity
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit verb IN (delete,deletecollection) | bin _time span=10m | stats count dc(objectRef.namespace) as namespaces values(objectRef.resource) as resources by _time user.username sourceIPs{} userAgent | where count>20 | sort - count

splunk.title: Namespaces and PVCs deleted
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit verb=delete objectRef.resource IN (namespaces,persistentvolumeclaims,persistentvolumes,customresourcedefinitions) | table _time user.username objectRef.resource objectRef.namespace objectRef.name responseStatus.code

splunk.title: Cloud disks deleted after PV release
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventName=DeleteVolume earliest=<deletion_time> | table _time userIdentity.arn requestParameters.volumeId sourceIPAddress
